vjimc-2003-cat2-01.title: Coprime polynomials (Bézout)
vjimc-2003-cat2-01.body:
Let $x$ be a vector with $(A+B+I)x=0$, i.e. $(B+I)x=-Ax$. We show $x=0$.

**Step 1.** By induction, $(B+I)^k x=(-1)^kA^kx$ for all $k\ge 0$: if it holds for $k$, then, since $A$ and $B$ commute,
$$(B+I)^{k+1}x=(B+I)(-1)^kA^kx=(-1)^kA^k(B+I)x=(-1)^{k+1}A^{k+1}x .$$
With $k=2002$ we get $(B+I)^{2002}x=A^{2002}x=x$. Also $B^{2003}x=x$. So with
$$p(t)=(t+1)^{2002}-1,\qquad q(t)=t^{2003}-1$$
we have $p(B)x=0$ and $q(B)x=0$.

**Step 2: $p$ and $q$ are coprime.** Over $\mathbb C$ two polynomials are coprime iff they have no common root. A root of $q$ satisfies $|t|=1$; a root of $p$ satisfies $|t+1|=1$. The circles $|t|=1$ and $|t+1|=1$ meet only at $t=-\tfrac12\pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i=e^{\pm 2\pi i/3}$. For these $t^3=1$, so $t^{2003}=t^{3\cdot 667+2}=t^2\ne 1$. Hence there is no common root.

**Step 3.** By Bézout's identity (Euclid's algorithm in $\mathbb R[t]$) there are real polynomials $r,s$ with $r(t)p(t)+s(t)q(t)=1$. Substituting $B$:
$$x=r(B)p(B)x+s(B)q(B)x=0 .$$
So $\ker(A+B+I)=\{0\}$ and the square matrix $A+B+I$ is invertible. ∎

vjimc-2003-cat2-01.title: Simultaneous triangularisation
vjimc-2003-cat2-01.body:
Regard $A,B$ as complex matrices. Commuting complex matrices can be brought simultaneously to upper triangular form: there is an invertible $S$ with $S^{-1}AS$ and $S^{-1}BS$ both upper triangular (a common eigenvector exists because $B$ maps each eigenspace of $A$ into itself; then induct on the size). If their diagonals are $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ and $(b_1,\dots,b_n)$, then the $a_i$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, the $b_i$ those of $B$, and $S^{-1}(A+B+I)S$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $a_i+b_i+1$. So it suffices to show $a_i+b_i+1\ne 0$.

From $A^{2002}=I$ and $B^{2003}=I$ we get $a_i^{2002}=1$ and $b_i^{2003}=1$, so $|a_i|=|b_i|=1$. If $a_i+b_i+1=0$, then $|b_i+1|=|a_i|=1$ and $|b_i|=1$, which forces $b_i=e^{\pm2\pi i/3}$ (the intersection of the two unit circles centred at $0$ and $-1$). But then $b_i^3=1$, and together with $b_i^{2003}=1$ and $\gcd(3,2003)=1$ we get $b_i=1$, a contradiction.

Hence all diagonal entries are non-zero, $\det(A+B+I)=\prod(a_i+b_i+1)\ne 0$, and $A+B+I$ is invertible. ∎

vjimc-2003-cat2-02.title: Write the areas as integrals
vjimc-2003-cat2-02.body:
Let $\chi_i:\mathbb R^2\to\{0,1\}$ be the indicator function of $D_i$ ($\chi_i=1$ on $D_i$ and $0$ outside). Since $\chi_{D_i\cap D_j}=\chi_i\chi_j$,
$$a_{ij}=S(D_i\cap D_j)=\iint_{\mathbb R^2}\chi_i(x,y)\,\chi_j(x,y)\,dx\,dy .$$
(All these functions are bounded, vanish outside a bounded set and are continuous except on finitely many circles, so the integrals exist.) By linearity of the integral,
$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_ix_j=\iint_{\mathbb R^2}\sum_{i,j}x_i\chi_i\,x_j\chi_j\,dx\,dy=\iint_{\mathbb R^2}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\chi_i(x,y)\Big)^2dx\,dy\ \ge 0,$$
because the integrand is a square. ∎

*Remark.* The argument shows more generally that the matrix $\big(\mu(E_i\cap E_j)\big)$ is positive semidefinite for any measurable sets $E_i$ of finite measure: it is the Gram matrix of the vectors $\chi_{E_i}$ in $L^2$.

vjimc-2003-cat2-03.title: Generating function and iteration
vjimc-2003-cat2-03.body:
**Step 1: convergence and a formula for the limit.** By induction $a_n\ge 0$, and $a_{n+2}-a_{n+1}=a_n/2^n\ge 0$; together with $a_0=0\le a_1=1$ this shows $(a_n)$ is non-decreasing. Hence $a_n\le a_{n+1}$ and
$$a_{n+2}\le a_{n+1}\Big(1+\frac1{2^n}\Big)\ \Longrightarrow\ a_{n+2}\le a_1\prod_{k=0}^{n}\Big(1+\frac1{2^k}\Big)\le \exp\Big(\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k}\Big)=e^2 .$$
So $(a_n)$ is bounded and monotone, hence convergent. Summing $a_{k+2}-a_{k+1}=a_k/2^k$ for $k=0,\dots,n$ gives $a_{n+2}=1+\sum_{k=0}^n a_k2^{-k}$, so
$$L:=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=1+\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{a_k}{2^k}=1+f\big(\tfrac12\big),\qquad f(z):=\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_kz^k .$$
Since $0\le a_k\le e^2$, the series $f(z)$ converges for $0\le z<1$, and $0\le f(z)\le e^2/(1-z)\le 2e^2$ for $0\le z\le\frac12$.

**Step 2: a functional equation.** Multiply the recurrence by $z^{n+2}$ and sum over $n\ge 0$ (all series converge absolutely for $0\le z<1$):
$$\sum_{n\ge0}a_{n+2}z^{n+2}=z\sum_{n\ge0}a_{n+1}z^{n+1}+z^2\sum_{n\ge0}a_n\Big(\frac z2\Big)^n,$$
i.e. $f(z)-z=z f(z)+z^2f(z/2)$, or
$$f(z)=\frac{z}{1-z}+\frac{z^2}{1-z}f\Big(\frac z2\Big).$$
For $z=2^{-n}$ this reads
$$f(2^{-n})=\frac{1}{2^n-1}+\frac{1}{2^n(2^n-1)}\,f(2^{-n-1}).\tag{$*$}$$

**Step 3: iterate.** Put $P_n=\prod_{k=1}^n(2^k-1)$, $t_n=\dfrac{1}{2^{n(n-1)/2}P_n}$ and $r_n=\dfrac{1}{2^{n(n+1)/2}P_n}$. We claim that for every $N\ge1$
$$f\big(\tfrac12\big)=\sum_{n=1}^N t_n+r_N\,f\big(2^{-N-1}\big).$$
For $N=1$ this is $(*)$ with $n=1$: $f(\frac12)=1+\frac12f(\frac14)$, and $t_1=1$, $r_1=\frac12$. If it holds for $N$, insert $(*)$ with $n=N+1$:
$$r_N f(2^{-N-1})=\frac{r_N}{2^{N+1}-1}+\frac{r_N}{2^{N+1}(2^{N+1}-1)}f(2^{-N-2})=t_{N+1}+r_{N+1}f(2^{-N-2}),$$
because $\frac{r_N}{2^{N+1}-1}=\frac{1}{2^{N(N+1)/2}P_{N+1}}=t_{N+1}$ and $\frac{N(N+1)}2+N+1=\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}2$.

**Step 4: pass to the limit.** Since $0\le f(2^{-N-1})\le 2e^2$ and $r_N\le 2^{-N(N+1)/2}\to0$, the remainder tends to $0$, so $f(\frac12)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty t_n$ and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=1+\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{2^{n(n-1)/2}\prod_{k=1}^n(2^k-1)} .$$
(Numerically both sides equal $2.17266875\ldots$) ∎

vjimc-2003-cat2-04.title: Chebyshev, Cauchy–Schwarz, then Fubini
vjimc-2003-cat2-04.body:
The integrand on the left is continuous on $(0,1]$ and bounded by $\max f/\min g$, so the left side exists.

**Chebyshev's inequality for integrals.** If $u,v$ are both increasing (or integrable and similarly ordered) on $[0,x]$, then
$$\frac1x\int_0^x u\cdot\frac1x\int_0^x v\le\frac1x\int_0^x uv .$$
*Proof:* $(u(s)-u(t))(v(s)-v(t))\ge0$ for all $s,t$; integrating over $[0,x]^2$ gives $2x\int_0^x uv-2\int_0^xu\int_0^xv\ge 0$.

**Step 1.** Apply it to $u=f$ and $v=g/f$ on $[0,x]$, $0<x\le1$: $\frac1{x^2}\int_0^x f\int_0^x\frac gf\le\frac1x\int_0^x g$, i.e.
$$\frac{\int_0^x f}{\int_0^x g}\le \frac{x}{\int_0^x \frac{g}{f}} .\tag{1}$$

**Step 2.** By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
$$\frac{x^4}{4}=\Big(\int_0^x t\,dt\Big)^2=\Big(\int_0^x\sqrt{\tfrac gf}\cdot t\sqrt{\tfrac fg}\,dt\Big)^2\le\int_0^x\frac gf\,dt\cdot\int_0^x t^2\frac fg\,dt,$$
so $\dfrac{1}{\int_0^x g/f}\le\dfrac4{x^4}\displaystyle\int_0^x t^2\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}dt$. With (1):
$$\frac{\int_0^x f}{\int_0^x g}\le\frac4{x^3}\int_0^x t^2\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}\,dt .\tag{2}$$

**Step 3.** Integrate (2) over $x\in(0,1]$ and swap the order of integration (the integrand is non-negative on $\{0\le t\le x\le 1\}$, so Tonelli's theorem allows it):
$$\int_0^1\frac{\int_0^x f}{\int_0^x g}\,dx\le\int_0^1 4t^2\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}\Big(\int_t^1\frac{dx}{x^3}\Big)dt=\int_0^1 4t^2\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac1{t^2}-1\Big)dt=2\int_0^1\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}(1-t^2)\,dt .$$
Since $f/g>0$, the last integral is at most $2\int_0^1 \frac{f(t)}{g(t)}dt$. ∎

*Remark.* The constant $2$ is optimal: for $f\equiv1$, $g(t)=t+\varepsilon$ ($\varepsilon>0$) the left side equals $\int_0^1\frac{2\,dx}{x+2\varepsilon}=2\ln\frac{1+2\varepsilon}{2\varepsilon}$, while $\int_0^1\frac fg=\ln\frac{1+\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$; as $\varepsilon\to0^+$ both behave like multiples of $\ln\frac1\varepsilon$ and their ratio tends to $2$.
